title: A Faith as Precious as Ours
subtitle: 2 Peter 1:1–4
description: A farewell letter opens level: a faith as precious as the apostles' own, everything for life and godliness already given, and promises that make partakers of the divine nature.
paragraphs: The letter opens with a name fuller than the one the first letter used. “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ.” Simon is the old name, the fisherman's name, carried in front of the apostle's name as if the writer wants both halves of his life on the page at once. Then he turns to his readers, and the first thing he tells them is the standing of their faith next to his own. They are the ones who “through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours.” As precious as ours: the faith of scattered believers he has never seen most of, weighed against the faith of an apostle who walked with Jesus, and the scales come out level. The ground of the equality is not their achievement. It is the righteousness of God himself, who gives the same faith at the same value to people at very different distances from the events. Late in his own letter Peter will call this his second letter to them, and he will say plainly that he knows his tent is soon to be laid aside. This book stands in the undated group of the series, with no date given and none invented, and it reads from its first line like a man setting his house in order: what these people have, and what they must not lose.

The greeting is short and it is not small. “Grace and peace be multiplied to you through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.” Multiplied, not merely wished. And the channel of the multiplying is knowledge, the word this short letter will use more than almost any other. Grace and peace grow as God and Jesus are known, not as circumstances improve, and the opening blessing sets the letter's whole economy in one sentence: what the readers need most is not new information about the world but a deeper knowledge of the one who called them.

Then comes the claim the rest of the letter stands on. “His divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence.” Everything is the daring word in it. Not most things, not the spiritual things alongside a gap the believer must fill from elsewhere, but everything required for life and godliness, already given, past tense, through the same knowledge the greeting named. The calling itself is described by what did the calling: he called us by his own glory and excellence, as if the beauty and worth of the caller were themselves the summons. A reader who believes this sentence has no standing invitation to go shopping for a supplement to the Christian life. The supply is complete. What remains is growth in it, and that is what the next lesson in the letter will take up, link by link.

Out of that glory and excellence come the letter's other great gift. “Through these He has given us His precious and magnificent promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.” The promises are called precious and magnificent, the same register as the faith called as precious as ours, and their purpose is stated in one of the boldest phrases in the whole New Testament: partakers of the divine nature. Peter writes it plainly and moves on, attaching it to the escape his readers have already made from the world's corruption, the rot that evil desires work in a person from the inside. The telling carries the phrase the way he leaves it, stated at full strength, neither explained down into something safer nor built up into a system he does not build. The shape of the verse is enough: corruption escaped, promises given, a nature shared.

Four verses carry the whole foundation, and the letter wastes none of them. A faith of equal value, grace and peace multiplied through knowledge, everything for life and godliness already supplied, and promises great enough to make their holders partakers of the divine nature. Nothing in the opening asks the readers to acquire a standing they lack. Everything in it tells them to grow in a standing they have, and the growth is Peter's next subject, a chain that starts at faith and ends at love.

title: Make Your Calling and Election Sure
subtitle: 2 Peter 1:5–11
description: The virtue chain link by link, fruitfulness against blindness, and the striving that ends in a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom.
paragraphs: Everything has been given; now the given things are to be grown. Peter's instruction begins with a reason and an effort: “For this very reason, make every effort to add to your faith virtue; and to virtue, knowledge; and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness, love.” The chain has eight links, and the grammar of it matters. Each quality is added to the one before it, as if the believer is supplying materials to a structure already founded, and the sequence runs from the inside out: faith at the root, virtue and knowledge and self-control forming the character, perseverance and godliness holding it over time, and the last two links turning outward toward people, brotherly kindness ripening into love. The effort is commanded at full stretch. Nothing about it is passive. But the adding is done to a faith that was received, not manufactured, and the supplies are added inside a life that divine power has already furnished with everything it needs.

Growth in the chain is not decoration. It is what keeps the knowledge of Jesus from going idle. “For if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The danger Peter names is not ignorance but fruitlessness: a person can hold the knowledge and produce nothing with it, like a field that knows the rain and grows no crop. The qualities must be possessed and increasing, both. A settled quantity is not the picture; a growing one is.

Against the growing believer Peter sets a diagnosis that is almost medical. “But whoever lacks these traits is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins.” The man without the chain cannot see far. His vision stops at what is near, and the cause Peter gives is a failure of memory: he has forgotten his own cleansing. The whole letter is a reminder because Peter believes forgetting is the root disease. A believer who remembers being cleansed from past sins sees distance; a believer who forgets it goes blind at close range, and the virtues starve in the dark he makes for himself.

So the section lands on its command, and the command is the episode's title. “Therefore, brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure. For if you practice these things you will never stumble, and you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.” Make sure is the work assigned to the hearers, and Peter attaches two promises to the practice rather than to a feeling: no stumbling, and a welcome at the end that is described in the language of generosity, a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom. The kingdom has a door and the door will be opened wide. Calling and election are God's side of the matter; the chain of virtues is the side the believers are told to work, and Peter holds the two together without confusing them.

Seven verses carry the chain, the warning, and the welcome. From here the letter turns personal. The man writing it explains why he writes as a reminder at all, and the reason is that he does not expect to be writing much longer.

title: Eyewitnesses of His Majesty
subtitle: 2 Peter 1:12–18
description: A dying man's reason for writing reminders: no fables, an eyewitness claim, and the voice heard on the holy mountain.
paragraphs: Now Peter explains the letter itself. “Therefore I will always remind you of these things, even though you know them and are established in the truth you now have.” Reminder is not an apology. The hearers know the truth and are established in it, and he intends to keep reminding them anyway, because the forgetting diagnosed in the last lesson is a standing danger for people who know. The verb is future and settled: I will always remind. As long as there is a Peter to write and a church to read, the reminders will keep coming.

His reason is his approaching end, and he states it in the picture of a tent. “I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of my body, because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me.” The body is a tent, temporary lodging, soon to be struck and folded, and Peter says the Lord himself made the timing clear to him. He does not say how, and the telling invents no scene and no conversation to fill that in. What he adds is his provision for after: “And I will make every effort to ensure that after my departure, you will be able to recall these things at all times.” The letter in their hands is that effort. It is written so that recall survives the writer, and the rest of the book will test exactly what the reminder is protecting them against.

Then the claim that the whole letter's authority rests on, stated as a denial first. “For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty.” Fables cleverly devised are what the apostles did not follow. Eyewitness is what they were. The power and coming of Jesus Christ, the very things the scoffers of the last chapter will mock as never arriving, are presented as things seen, not stories invented, and the seeing is specified in the next breath to one event and one mountain.

The event is carried in Peter's own compression, and the telling leaves it there: Jesus on the mountain received honor and glory from God the Father, and a voice came to him out of what Peter calls the Majestic Glory. The voice itself is quoted as Peter quotes it, standing as its own words: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” And Peter's attestation is personal and plural at once: “And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.” We heard it. We were with him. The transfiguration itself, the shining face and the garments and the prophets standing there, is told whole in the Gospel books of this series, where it belongs; this letter does not retell it. It does something narrower and, for its purpose, stronger: it puts a named man on the record as a hearer of the voice, staking the reminder's truth on his own ears.

That is as far as the claim goes, and Peter goes no further with it. He does not argue the mountain or describe it or defend it. He states the denial of fable, the eyewitness standing, the voice, and the hearing, and then he turns from what he saw to what everyone can read: the word of the prophets, more confirmed than ever, shining like a lamp until the day dawns.

title: A Lamp Shining in a Dark Place
subtitle: 2 Peter 1:19–21
description: The prophetic word as a lamp in a dark place, and how prophecy came: not by man's will, but men carried along by the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs: From the voice on the mountain Peter turns to the voice in the book, and he ranks the written word as the thing his readers can hold. “We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt.” The mountain experience is not set against the prophecy; it is set under it, confirming it, and what the hearers are told to do concerns the prophecy, not the mountain. “And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.” The picture is a lamp in a dark room, modest against the day that is coming but exactly what is needed until the day arrives. Attention is the command. The lamp does its work for the people who keep looking at it, and it shines in the dark place, not after the dark place is gone.

Then the rule for reading the lamp, introduced as the first thing to understand. “Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation.” Interpretation here is pointed back at the prophecy's origin, as the next verse explains: the prophet was not untying a knot of his own making or publishing his own reading of events. Peter guards the source before he guards the study, and the guard is absolute in form: no prophecy of Scripture, not one, comes that way.

The reason is the letter's shortest account of how Scripture came to be. “For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” Not by the will of man: the initiative is removed from the prophets as firmly as the fables were removed from the apostles. Men spoke, genuinely spoke, and as they spoke they were carried along, the way a ship is carried by the wind it hoists its sail to. Carried is Peter's word and the telling leaves its weight where he leaves it, a claim about bearing and direction, not a mechanics of dictation built on top of it. What the verse builds is a chain the whole letter will lean on: the same Spirit who carried the prophets is the one whose words the false teachers will twist and the scoffers will ignore.

Three verses, and the first chapter is done. Its shape is worth seeing whole: a faith as precious as the apostles' own, everything supplied, a chain to grow link by link, a dying man's reminders, an eyewitness voice on a mountain, and a lamp for the dark. Against that shape the second chapter sets its opposite number: men who deny, deceive, and carry nothing but their own appetites. Peter turns to them without pausing, and his first word is that they are not new.

title: False Teachers Among You
subtitle: 2 Peter 2:1–3
description: False teachers inside the congregation: secret heresies, the Master denied, crowds following, greed exploiting, and a verdict that does not sleep.
paragraphs: The second chapter opens by placing its danger in a long line. “Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you.” Among the people then, among you now: the threat is not invasion from outside but corruption from inside the congregation, and it is presented as a certainty of the church's life, not a possibility to be surprised by. What they bring arrives quietly. “They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them.” Secretly is the manner and destructive is the cargo, and the cargo's center is a denial of the Master himself, the one who bought them, a phrase Peter leaves standing in all its weight without pausing to untie it. The sentence carries its own consequence in its second half, split where the text itself breaks: the denial ends in “bringing swift destruction on themselves.” The destroyers of others are destroying themselves, and swiftly.

Their following is not small, and its cost falls on the truth's reputation. “Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed.” Depravity is the path and many walk it behind them, and the watching world reads the way of truth by the people who disgrace it. Peter names the damage plainly: the teachers will be believed by crowds and the truth will be blamed for them. The letter does not promise that false teaching stays marginal. It promises the opposite, and tells the beloved beforehand so that the size of the following will not be mistaken for a verdict on the teaching.

The motive is named without decoration. “In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words.” Greed is the engine and words are the tool, words made up to extract something from the hearers, the exploiting of people as a trade. Against the whole operation stands a court already in session. “The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep.” The verdict is old, Peter says, older than the teachers, still in force, and their destruction is pictured as a living thing that does not doze while it waits. The first lesson of the book said the supply for godliness never sleeps on the believers' side. The dark mirror of it stands here: neither does the judgment.

Three verses do the whole introduction: their lineage, their method, their motive, their following, and their sentence. What proves the sentence is not rhetoric is the record, and Peter turns to the record next, a chain of the old judgments that runs from fallen angels to a man rescued out of a burning city.

title: The Lord Knows How to Rescue
subtitle: 2 Peter 2:4–9
description: One long sentence of judgments: angels in chains, a world flooded and Noah preserved, cities ashed and Lot rescued, and a Lord who knows how to do both.
paragraphs: The proof is built as one long sentence of conditions, and Peter piles them up before he lets the conclusion land. “For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment.” The chain starts at the top of creation. Angels sinned, and their rank bought them nothing: no sparing, a casting down, chains of darkness, and a holding cell whose door opens on judgment day. The telling carries the verse in the words the text gives it, deep into hell and chains of darkness, and adds no map of that prison and no names for its prisoners beyond the ones the verse itself supplies.

The second link is the flood. He “did not spare the ancient world when He brought the flood on its ungodly people, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight.” Wrath and rescue sit in the same verse, as they will all the way down the chain. The world that perished is the world of the first letter's baptism passage, and Noah's title here is his preaching: a preacher of righteousness in a generation that heard and drowned. Noah's story stands whole in Genesis in this series, and Peter's use of it is a pointer, not a retelling: eight preserved out of a world, because God knows how to do both halves of the work at once.

The third link is fire answering the water. He “condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly.” Ashes are the exhibit. The cities were made into a standing example, a ruin with a lesson posted on it for every age after, and the lesson is forward-looking: what is coming on the ungodly has already been shown once at full scale. And out of the same fire comes the chain's second rescue: he “rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless.” Peter insists on Lot's righteousness twice in two verses, and explains its proof from the inside: “that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard.” Lot's torment is his credential. A man at home in Sodom would not have been tormented by it. Genesis tells Lot's whole compromised story in its own book, and Peter's compression here keeps to Peter's point: the Lord found a righteous man inside a condemned city and got him out.

Then the sentence Peter has been building finally resolves, and it resolves as knowledge: “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.” Knows how: the rescue of the godly and the custody of the unrighteous are both presented as competence, a skill God has already demonstrated three times in the record just read. The false teachers' destruction does not sleep because it is being competently held, and the godly under trial are not an unsolved problem because their rescuer has a track record. From the record Peter turns back to the teachers themselves, and the description that follows is the longest, ugliest portrait in the letter.

title: The Way of Balaam
subtitle: 2 Peter 2:10–16
description: Appetite and contempt, tongues bolder than angels, hearts trained in greed, and the ancestor of them all: Balaam, rebuked by a donkey.
paragraphs: The portrait begins with appetite and contempt, the two engines of the false teachers named in one breath: the punishment is “specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings.” Slandering glorious beings, the angels, is their boldness on display, and Peter answers it with a comparison that reverses the expected order. “Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord.” The beings with the strength to make the charges will not make them. The men without the strength make them freely. Reverence, in this passage, tracks with power rightly understood: the stronger the creature, the more careful the tongue.

Then the comparison that runs the rest of the portrait. “These men are like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed.” Reason is what they have surrendered. What rules them is instinct, appetite operating without reflection, and their end is stated in the flat language of animal control: captured and destroyed. Peter does not argue with their teaching at this point in the letter. He describes their condition, and the description is the argument: men who run on appetite cannot be followed by people who mean to run on knowledge.

Their social life is drawn as sharply as their doctrine. “The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you.” Broad daylight is the detail that lands: no shame, no hiding, the carousing done at noon. And the feasting is with you, at the congregation's own table, where a blot shows worst against the cloth. “Their eyes are full of adultery; their desire for sin is never satisfied; they seduce the unstable. They are accursed children with hearts trained in greed.” Trained is an athlete's word, practice and discipline, turned inside out: these hearts have done their exercises in greed the way the believers of the first chapter were told to make every effort in virtue. Two trainings stand in the letter, link against link.

The portrait closes by giving the teachers an ancestor. “They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness.” Balaam is the prophet who could be hired, and his wage-love is the teachers' wage-love in its oldest form. “But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.” A speechless animal spoke and a prophet was the one acting mad: the reversal is Peter's whole verdict on hired religion in one scene. Balaam's story stands whole in the Numbers book of this series, the blessings he could not help speaking and the wages he could not stop loving, and Peter's use of him here is a pointer and a sentence at once. The teachers have an ancestor, an animal that outspoke him, and a way that is named for where it ends. What they offer the people who follow them is the next subject, and it is an offer of water from an empty spring.

title: Springs Without Water
subtitle: 2 Peter 2:17–22
description: Springs without water, freedom promised by slaves, the last state worse than the first, and two farm proverbs to close the portrait.
paragraphs: The portrait ends with what the teachers actually have to offer, and the offer is pictured before it is argued. “These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them.” A spring without water is a promise that fails at the moment of need: the traveler arrives thirsty and finds the shape of relief and nothing in it. A mist driven by a storm looks like weather coming and delivers no rain. Both pictures are of almosts, forms of provision with the provision missing, and against them stands the reservation made for the teachers themselves, blackest darkness, held the way their destruction was held, in force and unsleeping.

Their method with the vulnerable is then named exactly. “With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.” Lofty but empty: the words sound large and carry nothing, the verbal form of the waterless spring. The targets are chosen with a predator's eye, the ones just escaping, new believers still wet from the flood they fled, enticed back through the very passions they are learning to leave. And the bait is a word the hearers want. “They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.” Freedom promised by slaves is the letter's sharpest piece of logic. The test of a liberator is his own chains, and a man mastered by his appetites has only one product to sell: his mastery, rebranded.

The worst sentence in the chapter is reserved for the people who took the bait and went back. “If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first.” Worse than at first is the comparison, and Peter does not argue it gently. “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them.” Better never to have known: the sentence stands at full strength in the letter, and the telling leaves it there, neither filing it down nor aiming it at any reader by name. Knowledge refused after knowledge received is treated as a heavier thing than ignorance, because the turning is deliberate in a way the first not-knowing never was.

Then Peter closes the chapter with two farm proverbs, and he lets them be as coarse as they are. Of these people, he writes, the proverbs are true: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud.” The first is Scripture's own proverb, from the book of Proverbs; the second is a saying of the farmyard, and Peter sets them side by side as equals for his purpose. The washed sow is the picture to sit with. The washing was real. So is the mud, and the going back is the animal's own motion toward what it prefers. Chapter 2 ends there, in the mud, without a softening word. The last chapter of the letter will lift its eyes from the teachers to the scoffers and from the present corruption to the coming day, and it will end higher than any chapter in either letter: with patience, with fire, with a new earth, and with growth.

title: Scoffers Will Come
subtitle: 2 Peter 3:1–7
description: The second letter names itself, the scoffers argue from sameness, and the record answers with water: a world formed by it and once unmade by it.
paragraphs: The last chapter opens by naming the book itself. “Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking.” Two letters, one purpose, reminder, and the line is carried exactly as Peter writes it, with the telling building nothing on it beyond what the letters themselves say. What the reminders recall is then defined: “what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles.” Prophets and apostles stand as the two banks of the same river, the foretelling and the commanding, and wholesome thinking is what gets stirred when a person stands between them and remembers.

Against that memory stands the last days' predictable voice. He writes that “in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Their scoffing is quoted in their own words, standing as its own speech: “Where is the promise of His coming?” And their argument follows in the same voice: “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.” It is an argument from sameness: the world has always run as it runs, the fathers died and nothing interrupted the running, therefore the promised interruption is a fable. Peter has already answered the fable charge on the mountain. Now he answers the sameness charge from the record, and his answer begins by naming the argument's method: they deliberately overlook. The overlooking is a choice, not an honest gap, and what is overlooked is water.

“But they deliberately overlook the fact that long ago by God’s word the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water and by water, through which the world of that time perished in the flood.” The earth itself was formed out of water and by water, and the same element that framed the world drowned the world of that time. Sameness is the one thing the record does not show. The world has already been unmade once by the word of God and remade out of the flood, and the God who spoke it then has spoken about the present order too. “And by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.” Reserved and kept: the same competent holding that keeps the unrighteous for punishment keeps the cosmos for fire. The word that formed and flooded is the word that reserves.

That is the whole rebuttal, and it is worth seeing how Peter builds it. He does not argue that the world feels unstable or that the promise is near. He argues from what has already happened under the same word: creation by water, judgment by water, and a standing reservation for fire. The scoffers' premise, an unbroken sameness from the beginning, is denied by the beginning itself. What remains is the scoffers' real question, which is not whether but why not yet, and Peter turns to it next with the most famous arithmetic in either of his letters: the calendar of God, against the calendar of the impatient.

title: A Day Is Like a Thousand Years
subtitle: 2 Peter 3:8–13
description: God's calendar against impatience, patience with a purpose, the Day like a thief, elements melting, and a new earth where righteousness dwells.
paragraphs: The question of delay gets its answer in one sentence of arithmetic, and Peter addresses it to the beloved, not to the scoffers. “Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.” The line runs in both directions, and both directions matter. A thousand years are like a day to the Lord, which answers the charge that he is slow: the interval that looks like an age from inside it is a day on his calendar. And a day is like a thousand years, which says the traffic runs the other way too: he can crowd into a day the weight of an age. The shape of the line comes from the Psalms, where a thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday when it is past. Peter takes the Psalm's measure and applies it to the promise, and the application is personal before it is cosmic: do not let this escape your notice.

Then the charge of slowness is met head on and redefined. “The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.” Not slow, patient, and the patience has a purpose clause that gives the delay its whole meaning: people perishing is what God does not want, and repentance is what the interval is for. The waiting is not an absence of action. It is mercy doing its work at the pace of human turning. Peter aims the correction at the beloved who might mistake the calendar, and a few verses later he will tell them to count this same patience as salvation itself.

What the patience is delaying is then described without any softening. “But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.” Like a thief: unannounced, in the night, taking the household by surprise, and the description that follows is carried exactly as the text gives it, down to the last clause, where other versions of the verse in English read differently; here the earth and its works are laid bare, exposed to sight, rather than consumed in the sentence. The heavens disappear with a roar. The elements are destroyed by fire. Nothing is held back and no date is attached, and the passage immediately does with the terror the thing Peter always does with it: turns it into a question about the people hearing it.

“Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat.” The dissolution of the elements is made a reason for holiness in the present, and the believers are even said to hasten the day they anticipate, a claim Peter states and does not explain, leaving the hastening where he leaves it, inside holy and godly conduct. And over the whole burning horizon stands the promise the chapter ends by looking toward: “But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.” Not a repaired old earth but a new one, and its defining resident is righteousness itself, dwelling there the way corruption once dwelt in this one. The fire is not the last word of the chapter. The address of righteousness is. One short closing remains: the diligence, the brother Paul, the guard, and the growth.

title: Grow in Grace and Knowledge
subtitle: 2 Peter 3:14–18
description: Diligence to be found spotless, a beloved brother named Paul, a guard against falling, and growth in grace and knowledge as the last word before glory.
paragraphs: The letter closes the way the whole book has taught its readers to live: in anticipation, working. “Therefore, beloved, as you anticipate these things, make every effort to be found at peace,” and then the two words the split in the verse sets off like a seal: “spotless and blameless in His sight.” Make every effort is the same strenuous phrase that opened the virtue chain in the first chapter. The last instruction of the letter is the first instruction of the letter, aimed now at the day of God instead of the chain: grow, strive, be found. The finding is God's; the effort is theirs; and the state to be found in is peace, without spot or blame, in his sight rather than in the world's.

Inside the diligence sits the letter's most personal paragraph, because it reaches across the early church to another apostle's desk. “Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him.” Our beloved brother Paul: the Galilean fisherman writes of the Pharisee from Tarsus with open affection, and credits his letters to the wisdom God gave him. “He writes this way in all his letters, speaking in them about such matters.” All his letters, about such matters, the patience and the promise and the day: Peter treats Paul's whole correspondence as known to his readers and on his own subject. Then the sentence readers have quoted ever since: “Some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.” Hard parts are admitted without embarrassment. The twisting of them is assigned to the ignorant and unstable, and Paul's letters are placed, in Peter's own phrase, with the rest of the Scriptures. The telling carries the sentence exactly as it stands and builds nothing on it: no list, no dates, no theory of how collections grew. An apostle testifying about another apostle's writings, near the end of his last letter, is the whole of the evidence and it is left whole.

The last warning returns to the letter's standing posture, foreknowledge as armor. “Therefore, beloved, since you already know these things, be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing.” Already know is the ground of the guard. The secure standing is real and can be fallen from if the guard drops, and the carriers-away are the lawless of the second chapter, still at their work in the last paragraph. Against falling, Peter sets one final, growing thing. “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.” Not hold still, not merely stand, but grow, in grace and in knowledge, the two currencies of the letter's opening greeting, where grace and peace were to be multiplied through knowledge. The circle closes: multiplied at the start, growing at the end.

And then the doxology takes the last word: “To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.” Both now and to the day of eternity: the glory runs across the whole interval the scoffers mocked, the long patience, the reserved fire, and arrives at the day when time itself gives way. The brief second letter ends there, with no farewell list and no greetings, only growth commanded and glory assigned. The man who knew his tent was soon to be laid aside spent his remaining strength on reminders, and the reminders outlived the tent, which is what he said he was making every effort to ensure.
